Title: i have seen some strange things around mit recently
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content:
a couple weeks ago, i looked out of my bedroom window to the east, and i saw something weird, but the angle out of my window wasn’t very good and i couldn’t really make out what it was.

later, i was walking in that direction (maybe i was going to cvs? not sure) and i got a better view. fluttering in the wind were five giant inflatable white balls, emblazoned with various logos. oh hey! i recognize that one! it’s the tetazoo squanch![1]

look at those balls

later, i was reading the tech[2] and saw the balls featured again:

now with some more context

one of my friends told me that one of their professors had mentioned the “newton’s cradle thing” in class. i guess that this makes sense – the balls had been up for a couple days, and anyone walking around building 56 or 66 or mit health or going anywhere east would’ve seen them.

then one morning, i looked outside and the balls were gone – like they’d never been there in the first place.

a couple days later, i was walking to fencing, which is hosted in the z.[3] as i stepped out of lobby 7[4] and walked down the iconic steps towards mass ave, i saw a strange box.

a friend sent me a picture of it being more intact

it looked like it’d seen better days – one of its doors was broken and its windows slightly shattered. but besides that it stood proudly, facing the thousands of students streaming out of the dome every hour.

the door says “tea party”. i wonder what this might be about?

my roommate sean was walking around west campus and saw that someone put a pumpkin on the top of kresge[5]

pumpkin

slightly zoomed in

…

……

idk man

my friends alivia and jonah were taking an early morning run when they saw a ufo (?) on killian court[6] this morning. they sent these pretty crazy pictures to a group chat i’m in – do you guys think that’s a cow right under the ufo?

bit closer

i was really sleepy today, so i skipped fencing, but as i made my way west for chemistry, i saw this sign on a wall:

i hope they got the milk they wanted..

huh. i wonder if that’s the thing alivia and jonah saw?

out of curiosity, i walked to killian court, but by the time i got there it was gone. i wonder what that was all about? maybe the aliens got all the milk they were looking for?

gone as quickly as it came

Title: a review of my first horror movie
Author: Joy X. '29
Article Content:
Cesare, the somnambulist.

I’ve never really been a traditional horror movie person. I don’t get the rush of adrenaline when I watch horror movies or get jumpscared—I just find it unpleasant. There is one exception: I absolutely love reading summaries of horror movies on Wikipedia; no blood, no gore, no jumpscares, no loud sounds, just pure plot and entertainment. It turns out that horror plots are kind of stupid and nonsensical without the visuals and music, especially when Wikipedia only gives you the bare bones of the plot, where scenes that are terrifying in theatres are reduced to less than a sentence. So, I’ve never really actually watched a horror movie, much less in theatres[1] …until this Halloween[2] .

In German class, two weeks before Halloween, our professor announced that the German Department had tickets[3] to a showing of Das Cabinet des Dr. Caligari, a silent horror film from 1920—with live accompaniment! Apparently it’s considered as the first psychological horror film. It sounded very interesting; I’ve never seen a film with live accompaniment before, much less the first film of its genre, so naturally, on All Hallows’ Eve, I found myself in the Boston Symphony Hall with some friends and fellow classmates from my German class. Here are my thoughts about it!

SPOILERS BELOW!

I’ll be giving some mild spoilers of the plot—if you want to experience the full 75 minutes of it for yourself, you can actually watch it on Wikipedia (wow, full circle–you can watch it on Wikipedia now! I love public domain :))

Music: 5.0/5

The music. Oh my god, the music was majestic. I mentioned earlier that the film had live accompaniment. I wasn’t sure what the accompaniment would be before I stepped into the Symphony Hall—would it be an orchestra? A pianist? I was absolutely delighted when I found a seat on the balcony and found myself facing a stage with a singular organ—I love the sound the organ; it’s probably my favorite instrument sound.

The acoustics in Symphony Hall were very good, and every dramatic scene was accompanied by a buildup and a dramatic BWWWUUUMMGGG[4] of the organ. The sound was absolutely majestic.

It was also very impressive to me that the organist could play for the entire 75 minute duration of the film without a conductor or (presumeably) being able to see the movie—it seemed like a long time to play, not to mention any mistakes in timing would lead to the cues being off for the entire rest of the film. Professional musicians amaze me. I could never.

Plot: 3.5/5

The story begins in a garden, with a young man, Franzis, telling a tale of his strange experience some years past to an unnamed old man. A town fair full of oddities, a doctor by the name of Dr. Caligari, and his exhibition—a mysterious sleepwalker named Cesare, who has been sleeping for twenty three years without break…

The night that Dr. Caligari arrives in the town, the town clerk is found dead, stabbed with a strange object in the night. The next night, Franzis and his friend, Alan, visit the Doctor’s attraction, where he unveils a cabinet with the sleeping somnambulist[5] a thin uncannily-proportioned man, eerily standing within.

The Doctor claims to his spectacle observers that Cesare knows all that has happened in the past, and can see into the future. He awakens Cesare, and urges his spectators to test him for themselves.

Curious, Alan asks Cesare. “How long will I live?”

He receives his reply: “Until the break of dawn…” Gasps of horror.

The next day, he is found dead. Stabbed in the side with a sharp object.

there it is, the titular cabinet!

There is of course more to the plot than this—I’ve left out most of the details in the second half of the film, which includes a kidnapping of a girl (by Cesare, the somnambulist) that both Alan and Franzis fancies, an asylum, and a twist in the last minutes. I’ll leave it to you to either find out about the plot by watching it or reading the Wikipedia summary :P

I was surprised at the plot twist—I was anticipating it, because at the beginning of the film, the organist spoke a few words, some of those words to the effect of “this is also a film where you can’t trust the narrator.” Hmmm…

I expected the plot twist to be [spoilers][6] but the actual plot twist turned out to be [spoilers][7] .

Overall, I found the plot to be interesting—I like the concept of a sleepwalker, and it was at times very suspenseful. I felt that it was a bit predictable and felt cliche at times, but I suppose it’s silly to blame a film that is the first of its genre to be predictable—after all, everything cliche is based off of it.

Scariness: 2.0/5

So a movie can’t naturally be very scary when, being a silent movie from that era, all the characters walk at 1.5x speed. At the climax of the movie, the film literally jumps a few frames, to a slightly humorous effect.

It definitely had a more disturbing than outright scary atmosphere. In particular, the set design was very distinctive—angular and somewhat claustrophobic, it looked almost cartoonish, more like something out of a Dr. Seuss story. I’m not a film analysis expert, but combined with the black and white coloring and occasional vignettes, I can say that it made for a very unique visual appearance and atmosphere.

is this where MIT got the inspiration for Stata Center?

if it were not black and white it would look like a Dr. Seuss setting

there was also this angular text that popped up between frames (as it was a silent movie, the dialogue appeared on the screen as text). the text says, “I had nothing to do with both the murders, so God help me” (there was another man accused of the murders that Cesare committed)

Also, the actor that played Cesare fit the role so well. His facial expressions were so creepy, and his lanky proportions were so uncanny. I wished there were more closeups of him, but the two closeup shots of him felt like he was staring into my soul.

this is the scene that my drawing of Cesare is based off of

Overall, I enjoyed the film! The atmosphere was spooky and great—not just the film, but the atmosphere in Symphony Hall was great too. The Hall was packed, and there were essentially three types of people there: old people dressed very fancily, as if they were going to an opera; random college students (us); and people dressed up in all sorts of different costumes, since it was Halloween, after all. I saw one woman posing in the hallway in a very good Cesare costume.

I loved that the film was in German—it gave me the opportunity to practice my German reading comprehension, though of course there were also English subtitles. I learned a lot of German words that day, but mostly words that had to do with murder and sharp objects.

I think it’s also my first time watching a movie this old—it’s crazy to think that this movie was released over a century earlier. After some poking around on Wikipedia, I found that most of these actors were born in the 19th century, and some died before WWII began. Their surviving descendents are likely around four generations down now. This film might even be the only footage of some of the lesser known background actors.

I’m glad that these films are still being played, and that we can still see, through the medium of film, through windows into the wholly different artistic styles of a world long in the past.

Footnotes:
[1] okay technically it was a symphony hall
[2] shhhh i'm behind on blogging okay
[3] MIT’s German Department is really into films, which I’m a big fan of—every fall for the past five years, they’ve hosted a German film series. I’ve only gone to one of them so far, a showing of Amrum, a story about a small village on the German island of Amrum in the last days of WWII
[4] how do I represent the sound of an organ in text…the question of the ages
[5] a synonym for sleepwalker
[6] A girl, Jane, was introduced before Alan’s murder, whom Alan and Franzis both loved. Before Alan’s death, Franzis and Alan had a whole conversation where Franzis told Alan something like “okay, let’s not stop being friends just because we love the same girl. We’ll let her decide”. Well, after Alan’s death, she has no choice. Up until the last five minutes of the film, I suspected that it would be revealed that Franzis killed his own friend and made up the story about the sleepwalker.
[7] the entire time, Franzis was a patient in a mental asylum. This was implied in a way that confused me because I wasn’t expecting it, and had to Wikipedia it afterwards to realize what it was hinting at

Title: my THIRD mit science bowl [liveblog]
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content:
when i was in high school, the thing that took up the most amount of my time was science bowl.[1] for hours upon hours every week i would find myself sitting in mr maine’s well-ornamented room after school (tuesdays and thursdays, until 6!), or back hunched leaning over my computer, thumb poised over my space-bar like a trigger, or closing my eyes and waiting for sleep as the seeds of questions and the skeletons of tournament brackets raced through my head.

picture of a nats competition stage!

my junior year mit scibowl was the first time that i remember coming to mit. it was a magical time – on friday night, we got dinner with alumni at saloniki’s; afterwards, steph and boheng, then freshmen in college (now juniors!), led me and my team and my friends on a wild-goose chase through the tunnels of mit. on saturday we played the tournament; after dinner with friends, we watched mit spinning arts club’s novemburn show and then my team stayed up playing party games until 4am.

in senior year, remembering all the fun i had the year before, i counted down the days until comp – until i could visit alumni, until i could play against disembodied friends from across the country, until i could hug people i hadn’t seen since summer.

there were probably more but i gave up on finding them

it’s not an exaggeration to say that science bowl is the main reason that i’m here at mit now. science bowl gave me the community and the enrichment and the challenge that i craved in high school; it gave me a reason to drag myself through the drudgery of a school day to make it to practice and dopamine and friends. with everything scibowl gave me, i was certain i wanted to give back.

mit scibowl runs on an annual cycle: question writing begins and is completed in the summer; editing starts with the school year, slowly transitioning into logistics; the tournament itself runs in mid-november, just as the air chills and starts to bite. this summer i wrote questions for biology, earth science, and energy, showing up to weekly playtesting meetings.[2]

school started and i started showing up to mit exec meetings. more question-editing, some logistics – me and some other frosh brainstormed mit scibowl’s first set of friday night activities, for students the night before the competition. yet even as i committed weekly time to scibowl, i eventually realized that somehow – without me really noticing its happening – it had slipped my mind, like a skate on ice. no longer did science bowl occupy dozens of hours of my brainspace a week.

yet i’ve still been counting down the days till this mit science bowl! now my excitement is driven not by my desire to play (because of course my role is no longer to play). now i want to put on a good show, help our tournament directors make sure everything runs smoothly. and honestly the biggest part is that my brother !!! and my mom !!! and friends !!! are coming !!! to visit :)

this year’s mit science bowl will be the largest ever. we’re inviting 60 teams of 5 players each to campus, relying on a team of over a hundred volunteers, games stretching from a crisp 9am[3] to 8pm if necessary. this year, i won’t be in the game rooms themselves;[4] instead i’ll be running whatever administrative errands are necessary to help keep the tournament going smoothly. over the next 24 hours, i’ll be writing about this event i love so much – now from a different perspective.

if you’re playing, good luck! i hope you have fun C:

if not, stay along for the ride :)

science PLATE (friday night activities)

this year we’re introducing science PLATE, which stands for Pre-tournament exhiLArating Team Events. since a lot of teams (like my high school’s) travel to cambridge ahead of time, we wanted to have something chill for the kids to do on friday night. this year we’ve prepared scrimmages (where teams play each other in friendly matches for practice), some board games, some light food, some printed puzzles, and (my personal favorite) karaoke!

right now we’ve just finished the opening ceremony, and the kids are playing a kahoot to get them somewhat oriented about how mit is laid out (so that they can find the rooms they need to play in tomorrow). do they know what room we’re currently in? (kinda) do they know what building the opening ceremony is in? (no)

look at all those answers

we’re in 4-163, which is like a lecture hall type room. the room is almost full with kids! most seats are taken. it’s nice to see that everyone is pulling up.

side note – something that’s kinda fried is that all flights nationally are grounded right now. this is bad for teams that were going to take red-eyes to get here, as well as some volunteers, like the connors from my high school team. they are stuck in the bay area… i really hope that flights are sorted out soon but i doubt it will be. this is pretty evil ngl

i suppose i should figure out some sort of karaoke layout? likely it is important for me to find the light switches and whatnot

7:35pm

okay after some brief technical difficulties i got karaoke working like thirty minutes ago! sound wasn’t working and youtube wasn’t loading on the shared screen, but it turns out restarting your computer fixes a lot of problems.

my theory of karaoke is that you need a critical mass of people singing before new people feel comfortable joining in. this is because all people are intrinsically awkward, and people who do science competitions in high school are especially so. luckily my awkward limbo was saved by the entire two teams of pioneer charter high who immediately lit up the room with their energy

we went through a lot of songs but i don’t remember all of them – sunflower, hot to go, riptide, beauty and a beat. we still have like an hour and a half left so i’m hoping that the high level of sound being emitted from this room will summon more children (the more the merrier!)

bonus points if you can guess the song!

9:44pm

PLATE is now over! i had a good time; the room was never empty and there was continuous songs basically from like 7:10 to 9, when we ended. unfortunately for admin-side the work isn’t over for the night.

usually we have lots of stuff set out ahead of time – brackets, room signs, etc – but the 3 hour flight stoppage has thrown a wrench into our plans. we have already had 3 teams that are guaranteed not able to make it all the way to boston because their flights got cancelled, and some of our volunteers (exemplified by my friends connor and connor) are stuck across the country, which means we need to shuffle volunteers around to make sure that all the rooms are staffed.

i was initially planning to go to my friend’s room but i think there is too much to do to justify that

hopefully i do not stay up super late because i really can’t function on little sleep :skull:

11:04pm

okay i am in my bed now preparing to sleep. there are still a lot of admin in stud working on things for tomorrow – finding 6 more boxes and 11 more extension cords, etc. we put off bracketing stuff and room signs until tomorrow morning at 6:30am, meaning that i have to be awake in less than 7.5 hours… i think 6:30 is the earliest that i have been awake in maybe half a year? barring plane stuff or whatever, and this is the first time i’m sleeping before midnight in a while.

i think as a competitor i really did not understand all the work that has to be done adminside. especially this year since we expanded our field by 25%, it is definitely a significant amount of extra stress (in the mechanical sense) that is not helping the structural integrity of our tournament

but also i am pretty optimistic that everything will be alright. i guess one thing that i prided myself on in high school was my general competence – my ability to handle a lot of different things generally well – and here i haven’t really yet felt that yet. i’m not the person at the head of this tournament, of course, but i think mit science bowl is somewhere where i can do my best in whatever needs to be done and smooth the path for competitors

good night and see you tomorrow morning!

tournament day!

6:52am

i am proud of myself for actually waking up. turns out that you can’t just gaslight your suprachiasmatic nucleus[5] into making you fall asleep earlier, and therefore i ended up going to sleep around 12:20.

but now i am with a bunch of admin in the bush room! uhaul with all our stuff is slightly delayed, meaning i am currently and briefly jobless. but after that my job is to carry stuff until 7:30; then i’ll start checking in teams (which is exciting!)

i will see the amount of functioning i can do on 6 hours of sleep. usually during full-lengths competitions we would try to take staggered naps during the competition – i wonder if i can take a nap today?

it’s so pretty outside but it’s soooo cold

10:44am

alright it turns out that i am modding! i just finished reading rr3 prisms vs asfa; i also read the first round in this room between greenwich 2 and troy from michigan. for our 2nd rr we had a bye because of last minute drops due to the flight stuff from last night so we just read the round for a 2v2 with the members of the team

even though i haven’t modded for a while, i think that i have gotten quite acclimated to it. i think i am doing an okay job enunciating and whatnot yay! i am slightly bad at calling stalls and blurts and whatnot but i think i am getting the hang of it. it is really fun to do all the introduction stuff from the other side… i don’t know. i think i have more deep thoughts about this but i’m too tired to express them right now

we’re hanging out with greenwich 2 right now because the other team hasn’t shown up! oh now they’re doing pushups wow

they’re 99% sure this is reggie and not romeo, who is an identical whale

11:01am

okay we’re lowkey mid-round but i really wanted to say this. we were doing icebreakers and the question was “if you were a vending machine what would you dispense?” all the kids went through and answered, and during the coach introduction a kid on farmington asked the coach (who is also his dad) to answer the icebreaker too.

the dad says, face deadpan, “if i were a vending machine i would dispense boys that listen to me”

GOTTEM

room erupts in laughter

1:27pm

lunch is over! i’m in room 4-257 modding the first round of double elimination with basis bellevue and weston. i had a nice lunch break – i ate a little bit of pizza, then broke down our rr room, and then went to get takeout with my high school team. hung out with mod friends during lunch too! yay!

yayyy

1:59pm

de1 over! some of these high schoolers are really scary. we’re currently waiting for the next team to show up

i didn’t have time to explain this before, but double elimination is really the heart of a science bowl competition. double elimination has real stakes: if you lose two games, you’re out. back when i used to compete my heart would do crazy things.

i was talking with people about this at lunch, but i really missed the atmosphere of a science bowl tournament. people are so eager and so invested and everyone is so social. especially i love it when the team members are so supportive of each other when they do a good buzz – i think the interpersonal interaction is really what i missed about this

praneel, a senior from james clemens high school, asked me if i miss competing. i don’t really think i do? i think what i really miss is the feeling of walking into a room and waving at people i know, and smiling through the introductions and hearing science and being awed by people’s cleverness, and this is all stuff that i can do from the moderator’s desk.

basis bellevue from bellevue, washington, with their mascots miso, turt (short for turtle), and cin (short for cinnamon)

3:12pm

usually in bowl games spectators are not supposed to be on electronic devices, but i am staff so i think it is okay BUT if you are reading this you should NOT be on your device during a match!

i have a bye this round (since i’m modding a winners bracket room), so i’m silently sitting in the audience of a game that my high school’s team is playing. they seemed a little annoyed that they lost in de2 – i think they wanted to stay in the winner’s bracket longer – but it seems like they’ve gotten back in the swing of things. right now the score is 126-44 in their favor against lambert.

i don’t know – i’ve been texting my friends throughout and it seems like there is a good number of upsets going on. there are so many good teams in the loser’s bracket, but i guess there just isn’t enough space in the winner’s bracket for all the teams that deserve to be there. i remember now how stressful science bowl can be: it’s really easy to get caught up in the adrenaline of it and to overworry and to get distracted from the matter at hand. i’m really proud of all of these kids for fighting through the tiringness and the worryingness that tournaments like this can bring

personally i am starting to be very tired lol…. i drank all of my thai tea (yay! caffeine!) but that can only sustain you for so long. i also didn’t eat very much lunch and am becoming hungry

i missed when they were shaking hands

5:19pm

view on the way to dance troupe in the stud

brief interlude for dance troupe practice complete, and i’m back in 4-270 to watch my high school’s team play basis independent silicon valley. dance practice was not as bad as i feared given that i skipped the last two practices and that second showings was terrifying. again keep your eyes open for a dance-themed blog in the future

back to the present – oh my god it is fricking TERRIFYING to watch scibowl. my coaches and my parents always used to say this but there is something worse about watching your kids go into battle and not being able to do anything about it except trust. deep breaths

also i’m lowkey really hungry :skull: but there is still time remaining before dinner so ggs

6:27pm

that round finished – my high school ended up winning that one, but lost a really close game right afterwards, finishing top 4 which is quite good. i’m really proud of them :)

after the basis silicon valley game i decided that it was wayyyy too fricking stressful to watch my team so i decided to watch winner’s finals instead, between blair and prisms. this was also such a CLOSE game like it was tied at the third to last question and decided by the last one. i think a lot of people probably did not expect prisms to come this far because of past performance, but they have done extraordinarily well

even when it’s not teams i super care about it is sooooo stressful :skull:

also good news i was able to delay the restaurant reservation after i looked at when the schedule had this tournament ended. yay!

okay match is starting aaaaaaaaa

SCIENCE BOWL IS WAY TOO STRESSFUL

7:15pm

finals time between basis bellevue and prisms. prisms is undefeated and only needs to win one game to win the tournament; basis bellevue needs to win back to back.

i am eating tangerines. i think my hunger was really not helping how stressed i was so i am glad that i am eating food. i think i am now more relaxed and able to enjoy scibowl!

i have really appreciated seeing all of the friends i’ve made over the past three years. excited to see finals C:

it’s the day after, now

11:47am

i woke up like 20 minutes ago. last night i got swept away into a world of eager friends and shows about the differences in opportunities available to youth in urban and rural china[6] and didn’t really have the opportunity to blog as i went. but i’d like to offer a brief recap:

- finals was real fun; both teams (and especially my friends on these teams) played incredibly! it was a nailbiter final that came down to the last question and everyone involved should be proud of their performance. i am eternally awed by the knowledge and quickness of scibowlers
- closing ceremony where we learned that the exec members averaged like 4.1 hours of sleep or something the night before the competition
- i wrangled up a bunch of kids to take them to a reunion dinner that we often have at dumpling house, a chinese restaurant on mass ave (but a bit more on the harvard end). this was one of the things that impressed/shocked/surprised me and my other freshman friends – we used to come to these dinners and be the youngest in the room, and the college students then would order for us and tell us stories about college and we would just listen, and now somehow WE are the ones organizing dinner and figuring out how to order and having to be the social lubricant between the chinese restaurant staff who are very unimpressed with our lack of skill with ordering even though WE are not chinese. but overall i think it was a good dinner :)
- walked back to mit. here i spent 30 minutes figuring out where my kids and my mom are going to stay tonight, because their flight got cancelled and they need a place to be. i eventually figure out that we will all have a sleepover on my floor! yay. i am so grateful to the people i live with for being so kind and understanding[7]
- talked for a while with my friend freddy, who over the past 3 years has become someone i feel i can confide anything in.
- went back to my dorm and stayed up until 2 watching link click with my friend angelina, who’s visiting to volunteer from berkeley, and xinlan and audrey, two tetazoo sophomores. this show is kinda ridiculous and i do need to watch more. fell asleep in walounge

while talking to freddy i think i figured out some of my thoughts about scibowl. it is really beautiful to come back to a community you find that you have grown past and to yet still see the same things – the curiosity, the enthusiasm, the vulnerability – that you loved about that community, now in a younger crop of somewhat-strangers. and i feel that this is what makes me want to keep staffing mit scibowl: the idea that, even though it is not a glamorous job, that i can put in work to run an event that brings these brilliant kids together for a double-dose of fun and growth.

Footnotes:
[1] science bowl is a government-sponsored competition where you win if you push buttons faster and answer questions more correctly than the other team does. want to see how it works? go watch last year’s mit scibowl finals video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uW-jb2qBkXo
[2] when i could - sometimes travel got in the way
[3] volunteers need to be ready by 8 - i don't know when the last time i woke up before 8am was
[4] or at least i’m not planned to be
[5] a part of your brain that regulates circadian rhythm
[6] aka link click
[7] hotel rooms cost like $500 rn :skull:
Subtitle: …but now i’m on the other side

Title: Slinging π’s
Author: Nicholas R. '29
Article Content:
The other day I was walking to Next House. I was by myself, headphones on, in the middle of a downpour—completely soaked yet steadfast in my journey to eat the best dining-hall chicken tenders and fries on campus.[1] I was hungry. Food was on my mind.

On my way past the tennis courts I was seized by a string of memories. First, it was of pizza. Then, naturally, it was of when I first stepped foot on MIT’s campus, over four years ago…

It’s freshly summer, and I’m a soon-to-be sophomore in high school. It’s my second summer working at a local pizza restaurant called Pizza Barbone. I started as a dishwasher, but this summer I’ve been promoted to pizza-maker. In addition to the restaurant itself, Barbone has mobile pizza-oven trucks and offers catering across Cape Cod and, occasionally, the Greater Boston area.

I’m on my very first catering event, admittedly a bit nervous as I ride shotgun in the truck with my boss, Jason. After over an hour of driving, we’re just now entering the city; we make our way through the Boston traffic and are soon rolling down Memorial Drive, past Maseeh and other less castle-like dorms. We park the truck in front of a fraternity[2] and are greeted by our clients: a group of college-aged guys, presumably students in the frat. We begin setting up our workspace and preparing the pizzas. Given that I’m still early on in my pizza-making journey, Jason guides me through the process of stretching the dough and topping it. I feel the dough awkwardly sag and slip through my fingers—I didn’t yet have the proper technique[3] to prevent it from tearing or stretching too thin. After forming some questionably-shaped pies,[4] I start topping while Jason feeds the glowing brick oven some wood chips. Once the fire is going, the pizzas get fed to the oven, and the dough rises and bubbles, forming a beautiful Neopolitan crust.

I watch the freshly-cooked pizzas be carried inside the building, which has slowly been filling up with guests during our prep. I hear standard fare from a college-party playlist[5] blasting through speakers, competing with the cheerful shouts and chatter from the people inside. In that moment I feel as if I’m staring at an exhibition: this is what college looks like, just as I have seen in the movies. I look behind me. There’s people walking by, one is repping an MIT hoodie. There’s some other figures on the court, playing tennis. The sun tries peeking through the overcast.

That’s about where the memory ended, just as I was clouded with thoughts of chicken tenders and fries.

I hadn’t thought about that moment in a long time. It’s strange and maybe poetic to think about how I was staring at my future, in a way. That was really the first time I remember thinking about college, or what I would do beyond high school, in a serious way. It still felt so far away. I still had at least a few more summers to work at Barbone, after all. And that restaurant job was very formative for me: I learned many cliché yet important things about myself and working with others in a professional setting. Four years later, I’m here and I still have much to learn. The more you see, the less you know.

Anyways, I want to end this meandering blog with a small piece of unsolicited advice. To current or prospective applicants: don’t shy away from talking about high school jobs in your college applications. If it was formative to yourself as a person, then I’d argue it’s worthy of mentioning—whether it is particularly glamorous or not, academic or not. I remember feeling hesitant about including my “silly” summer job on my applications. I thought it might be better to include something that was academic-leaning, but I realized there was nothing that I could’ve replaced it with that felt as personally significant as slinging pies.

Title: Something to believe in
Author: Janet G. '27
Article Content:
MIT is not known for its polish or ease. We are a cramped-up campus of noisy, scrappy, endless construction; we are college students who are too busy to look happy or well-groomed; we only really have two types of weather, too-hot-and-humid and too-dark-and-cold.

But we work with what we have: we make affectionate nicknames out of our buildings and all their odd shapes and histories; we embrace the camaraderie that comes from drinking the firehose; we hold onto the brief weeks when the sun peeks through the clouds, with bright blue skies and golden foliage and the shimmering Charles, and remember the other meanings of IHTFP.

We work with what we have, and we make something out of it.

the shimmering charles

Let me show you something from September 19th. Come with me as I jump out of bed at 10am on a Saturday morning when I would otherwise be asleep; follow me through the dewy grass and under the big white tent that seems to have sprouted up on Kresge lawn overnight, and collect an engraved navy badge and an illustrated tote bag from some beaming sleep-deprived organisers in bright yellow hoodies; talk to the students lugging suitcases and neck pillows next to you and learn that they flew over from Berkeley or Illinois or Switzerland to attend this hackathon; join a thousand people in Kresge Auditorium to listen to 3Blue1Brown give his first in-person talk at MIT since COVID; follow the crowd outside past the laser-cut and heat-pressed wonderland-themed flags adorning the lightpoles; walk down the brick path and into the Z Center, [1] and look at how the grey and silver walls are now plastered with pastel streamers, shiny balloons, and jumbo-sized handmade playing cards; pick up a macaron from the snack stand and then put it down upon realising it’s just really well-made clay; go into the Johnson Ice Rink, the thing you might know as a grey, cold, concrete, hollow beast, and realise that it’s suddenly been taken over by rows and rows of pastel tables and pink lights and balloon arches and great big projector screens, and you could call it beautiful.

September 19th was the first day of my last HackMIT, the first one that I’ve attended and not organised. This blog is about HackMIT, the club I spent three years organising and directing. It is also about my life, the institutions I’ve been involved in, and how we’ve shaped each other.

I’ve been working on this blog for a year now. There’s always more I could improve on, more days I could spend writing, rewriting, revising it. But I’ve sunk enough time into it, and I need to move on. So even when there’s more to do, even when something is precious to you, we work with what we have, and sometimes we have to let things go.

To understand how HackMIT mattered to me, you first need to understand who I am.

I spent the first 18 years of my life living in Hamilton, New Zealand. Hamilton is the fourth-largest city in New Zealand, but most people stop caring after the top three.[2] All the schools I went to were decile 5, certified average by the New Zealand education system. I never did out-of-school extracurriculars and spent most of my childhood rolling around in dirt, surfing youtube, and reading webnovels. I was the only second grader at my school asked to take a talent aptitude test, but they never followed up; I was nominated for Sports Girl of the Year at school because I won cross country, but only because the fastest girl fell over in the middle of the race; I lucked my way into the top three of my regional spelling bee, but proceeded to be the first person to get eliminated at the national bee. [3]

A stereotype is that MIT students are all labelled as exceptional from a young age: gifted, talented, prodigy. I was none of these things; I was an average kid who was smart enough, but only in my decile 5 school in the fourth-largest city in a small island country people don’t even remember to include on maps.

The only label I could describe myself with was hungry.

I was hungry to prove myself, and I jumped at every chance I had for a competition, which was not often when you’re from Hamilton. I never seemed to be the best, but I was relentless: I got a 0 on the maths olympiad entrance exam and came back for three more years; I spilled half the sample over my biology exam paper and finished my writeup on the soggy pages anyway; I was told by my junior debate teacher that I needed to “accept that [I] won’t always get a chance to speak when [better debater] needs the training opportunity more,” so I watched practice speeches on my own every day. I never won anything—always honourable mention, top 40, second place—but I never stopped trying. Honourable mentions can make it into the maths olympiad national camp, top 40s can win IBO[4] silver medals, second places can captain the national debate team.

Maybe I’m just a typical[5] middle child. My parents were always comfortable with my mediocre successes, since it allowed them to squabble and fuss over other things—my siblings, their jobs, each other. They reacted to all the achievements I brought home in the same way: a pleasantly surprised acknowledgement that lasted between ten and fifteen seconds. They had a stronger reaction when I told them that I wanted to apply to American colleges:
“Why would you want to do that? America is far. Also, you’re probably not going to get in anyway.”

They weren’t wrong. I was an aid-needing international student applying to top schools. So I leaned into the labels that would make me admissible: biology olympian, debater, theatre nerd, quirky kiwi. Fitting your life into a thousand words of application materials can feel like training to be a contortionist, but it was necessary to stand out as an applicant in a sea of thirty thousand.

When I got into MIT, I called my parents about it. The first thing my mum said was,
“How much does it cost? Why can’t you just do medicine at the University of Auckland?[6] You’d be a pretty decent doctor.”

But I saw a new identity tied to an institution that I’d barely dared to dream about. It would open doors, give me the resources and community to accomplish feats I couldn’t even imagine, and free me from needing to settle for the option my parents thought safest. I was going to prove my parents wrong: I wasn’t going to be a decent doctor comfortable with mediocre successes. After heated arguments, angry tears, and a generous financial aid offer, I was ready to call myself an MIT student.

My initial vision of an MIT student may have been overambitious: they were geniuses but also studious; they were firehose drinkers but also effortlessly organised; they were party animals but also led five clubs at once.

I thought it was doable; after all, I got into MIT. It couldn’t be that hard, right?

But MIT humbles everyone, whether you like it or not. I failed a 6.100A[7] quiz in my first semester and pulled a bunch of all-nighters over 8.01[8] psets. I tried out 6-7 clubs and still dropped basically all of them. I hated debating in the APDA format,[9] I got too afraid of the Shakespeare memorisation commitment, I wasn’t inspired to write poetry anymore, and I couldn’t afford to budget the number of hours required to enjoy Acapella and Mock Trial.

HackMIT was going to be just another club on the list. I forgot to apply to participate during the summer. I went to the organiser application info session only because friends said there was free boba. I also forgot about the organiser deadline, and only remembered when I saw a friend applying in the flounge at 10pm. I debated whether the long application was worth my effort, then wrote the app in 30 minutes and submitted at 11:50pm. I almost missed my interview the next day, and while I was excited in my response to the acceptance email, I was still thinking about the other applications I needed to fill out while I waited with the other new members to enter the welcome meeting.

Everything changed the moment I walked into the room. We were surrounded by cheering from Lili, Albert, [10] and the rest of the team, and they kept the energy throughout the entire evening: we went through a million introductions with everyone’s names and class titles, a huge spreadsheet with comic sans and fluorescent colours and signup slots going from 6am to 9pm, an endless list of tasks, a countdown of five days until my first HackMIT, a vision of the chaos to come, and somehow all of it was getting transcribed by Albert at 200 wpm. It was then that I decided this community was for me, and I would do everything I could to become embedded in it.

But wait—what does HackMIT even do?

HackMIT is a student club at MIT which runs two hackathons a year.[11] HackMIT is also the name of our flagship collegiate hackathon hosted in the fall, while Blueprint is a hackathon for 300 high schoolers hosted in the spring. To disambiguate between the club and the hackathon, we will from now on call the club Hack. To run the events, we have a very structured form of leadership: team members are led by committee heads, who are led by one director during the Blueprint-planning cycle, and two directors during the HackMIT-planning cycle.

We start the school year with HackMIT, which is led by two co-directors. After HackMIT, the senior co-director retires, and the new solo director runs Blueprint, our high school hackathon. The team plans through fall and winter to run Blueprint in the spring, and director elections happen after Blueprint to elect a new junior co-director. The two co-directors then lead the team through spring and summer to plan out HackMIT in the fall, the now-senior co-director retires, and the cycle repeats.

Blueprint 2024: learning the ropes

Onboarding at my first welcome meeting was chaotic, but that’s just how Hack is: it skews younger as a club,[12] so it trusts and expects new recruits to pick things up and run with them, whether you’ve had the relevant experience or not. This also informs the leadership structure: you can apply to be a committee head right after you join, and you can be trusted enough to be selected.

I was one such case: I ran for head of corporate relations right after HackMIT 2023, five weeks into freshman fall. I had to learn to scope out project timelines and coordinate with other committees, run weekly meetings and encourage team members when they were unmotivated, and balance our efforts between student outreach and corporate sponsorships. It was challenging. But in the end, I was proud of how Blueprint 2024 turned out.

It was now time for the next cycle of elections, and I had a lot of thinking to do.

Freshman year

I struggled a lot in freshman year. Some of the issues were about Hack, some of them were about moving ten thousand kilometres away from home and learning to live by myself, some of them were about being an MIT student. Everyone else seemed to be a great MIT student: taking more advanced classes while still doing well in them, landing internship offers at [Big Tech firms], doing meaningful research through UROPs.

So when I was thinking about running for director in the spring, I was also asking myself: What have I done with my life? I’d dropped all but two of my clubs. I could barely get through a pset without asking for help from friends. I hated the career fairs and had nothing to tell the companies. I found a research opportunity for the summer, but didn’t have much relevant experience and wondered if I would get anything out of it. It felt like all I was doing was struggling in my classes, feeling unhirable, and organising for Hack.

So in a way, Hack director was a label I felt that I needed: it was compensation for everything else that I hadn’t done. I wasn’t being a studious researcher, a technical intern, or an academic weapon. I was just a jobless quirky kiwi who did stuff with Hack.

I told my parents that I would show them just how much more I could do as an MIT student. What was I going to tell them now?

Director elections

I really wanted to become a director. I loved the club, and I had Opinions that I wanted to enact, but a big motivator was the insecurities I built up in freshman year, and I’m not going to deny that I felt competitive about it. After all, I spent years grinding for all-or-nothing competitions. But as I talked to the older directors and thought about why I wanted to run, I learned to embrace a different perspective: being a director is not just a title for your resume and ego, but a serious commitment that you will have to make sacrifices for. It is a role that you will grow a lot in, and you will be contributing to a community that you love, but the directorship isn’t the only role in Hack which provides that kind of fulfilment: committee heads also get a lot of leadership experience, and committed team members can also heavily shape the direction of Hack and get credit and growth for important projects. There are trade-offs to everything.

Two of my closest friends from Hack, Maggie and Alison, also ran for director. We doodled on the chalkboard, jumped up and down together to shake off our nerves, and coordinated “theme songs” that we would play when we entered to speak with the team. I was still nervous, but I knew that I could contribute to Hack as either a committee head or director, and I would get to work with Maggie and Alison, so these elections were going to turn out great regardless of the results. The point of director elections is to show the team a vision of what Hack will look like under your leadership, and to trust in their decision for the future they’re most excited about.

When I was announced as the newest director, Maggie and Alison swarmed me in a group hug, and we were once again jumping up and down together. They became some of the best committee heads who I’ve worked with, and are still some of my closest friends to this day.

After elections, I wrote in my notes app:

1. i am now director and that means that i have the weight of a team on my back. i have to be stronger with more personal resolve so that i can actually survive under all my responsibilities.
2. the people who run for hack director are also super passionate and i’m so excited for hack cycle heads and yayyyy

Becoming director was the biggest responsibility of my life; there was no turning back now. I couldn’t wait for the next 1.5 years. I told myself I’d do everything: I was going to lead the community, scale up the hackathon, and do whatever it would take to be the best Hack director possible.

HackMIT 2024: how to be a director

An institution is a relatively stable collection of rules and practices, embedded in structures of resources that make action possible – organisational, financial and staff capabilities, and structures of meaning that explain and justify behaviour – roles, identities and belongings, common purposes, and causal and normative beliefs. (March and Olsen, 1989, original emphasis)
— Why Institutions Matter, Vivian Lowndes and Mark Roberts

I joined as the 13th director to lead Hack. There had been over a decade of knowledge, mistakes, and adaptations built up before I arrived, and I spent the first few weeks as director absorbing as much knowledge as I could. At the time, this all felt like a slog through long conversations and notes app logs and Google Docs dating back years, but now I can formalise it: there were rules, practices, and narratives I had to learn, because these were the ways in which institutions (Hack) do their work (run a hackathon).

As the co-directors of Hack, Albert and I jumped into 6+ hours of meetings each week, for the committees, the team-wide generals, and syncs between us and committee heads. We started negotiating with MIT admin for various different things that we needed from them: overnight venue access, sponsorship packet approvals, so on and so forth. We pored over previous iterations of meeting notes to determine how we wanted to structure our general meetings, figuring out the messaging that we wanted the entire team to buy into: why do we spend so much time working on a hackathon? What does it mean for a hackathon to be good for the hackers? How do we want people to remember this hackathon?

Aside from all the director-specific problems, I learned much more about all the different committees in Hack. Every committee had distinct problems at scales that I’d never quite encountered before. We designed a new architecture to merge our major devops platforms, we experimented with new ways to make the theme more design-focused rather than illustration-focused, we negotiated with startups and tech firms to acquire hundreds of thousands of dollars, and we negotiated with MIT admin and restaurants and merch vendors to spend it. I had the resources to solve these problems, and I understood why people found power to be addicting. I could make things happen and it was awesome.

I leaned in, and let the title of Hack director consume my life. I quit ESP,[13] the only other club I was in, stopped applying to jobs since I’d found my summer UROP, and spent all day outside of classes thinking about how to do more with Hack. Every bit of work I put in was reflected in our progress towards HackMIT 2024.

It wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows. I felt guilty about dropping the ball for ESP multiple times. There were days when I got back home after a day of class or a day in the lab, and had to resist the urge to rot in bed in order to sit through 3+ hours of meetings or battle a spreadsheet. I learned to manage my own emotions, to organise my time, and to communicate firmly but kindly to people when they slacked off. Hack was the reason I got out of bed, my doomscrolling mechanism, and the catalyst behind most of the ways in which I grew.

how to say goodbye, part one

HackMIT 2024 came and went. The play-by-play is in the old blog that I wrote. What I remember from it now is the pride that swelled in me as I stepped onto the Kresge stage; the chaos of running around during judging; rolling around in the moving carts as we wound down after a long day. I remember sitting with Albert and Emily [14] in MacGregor after the hackathon ended, ordering burgers and fries from Tasty Burger and eating them with dining hall ketchup packets we saved, laughing about not being on the same wavelengths, thinking about how this was now the end of an era.

It might be an understatement to say that I was devastated when Albert left. He defined Hack as I had known it. I relied on him for advice both inside and outside of Hack, and we were two peas in a pod: sitting together in every meeting, always a topic to discuss, always a new joke to tell. Being a director was hard, but I knew that I could always rely on him when I didn’t want to run a meeting, or when I didn’t know how to have a difficult conversation, or when I just didn’t know how to do a certain task. Now that HackMIT was over, I had to run Blueprint by myself, and I had big shoes to fill.

Blueprint 2025: how to take on independence

Most major hackathon organisers only organise one hackathon a year: the amount of time required to invest in a thousand-person hackathon on top of school, work, and life is already a huge commitment. Still, we organise two hackathons and constrain ourselves to ~7 months for HackMIT. How does this high school hackathon justify the cost of needing to work all year round while compressing organising timelines for our flagship hackathon?

It’s because Blueprint is awesome. We teach high school students CS and hardware and make things for the sake of it, and we get to support educational access and give back to the local community. Having an extra cycle in the year also gives the organising team more opportunities to lead (e.g. allowing me to be a committee head before becoming director), grow (e.g. going through more iterations of the design / logistical / manufacturing processes), and experiment (e.g. testing out new initiatives at a smaller scale with lower stakes).

example: we prototyped a 3d website for the first time in blueprint '24

the older directors liked it :))

Where I learned a lot through co-directing my first HackMIT, I grew a lot through directing my Blueprint: I didn’t have a senior co-director to defer to when I wasn’t sure what to do, and had to take full responsibility for all my decisions and mistakes. I established new onboarding systems, tried out different team management methods, and ran meetings with my humble 120 wpm[15] and not-so-humble voice.

I initially imposed a lot of leadership baggage on myself. The team could lean on their committee heads when they struggled with work, the heads could lean on me, but I needed to be strong for everyone, so I couldn’t rely on anyone else, right? After my first Blueprint meeting as director, I packed up my laptop and felt a little hollow: it was just like my first meeting for HackMIT 2024, except now Albert was never going to walk back to BC[16] with me to plot together. I guess this is the life of a solo director. But after everyone else had left, I saw that Claire[17] had stayed behind for me. We walked, arm in arm, back to BC, and we yapped about Hack and life and everything else, and the hole in my heart was filled.

I soon learned that I was wrong about being alone. My committee heads came to me for advice and final decisions, but I also learned to be vulnerable and rely on them when I needed help. The team also supported (and challenged!) me: Eddie and Nicholas stepped in from a different committee to manage a logistics task when we didn’t have enough people; Adam and Maggie pushed back on my harsh messaging around tardiness when I should have been more considerate of people’s lives outside of Hack; Teresa helped moderate an argument I had with our umbrella club when things got too heated. I was often overzealous about the things I could do and got stuck in my own head, and I learned to be more humble, understanding, and stable as we went through Blueprint 2025.

Sophomore fall

Sophomore fall was overwhelming in more ways than just solo-running a hackathon. I was taking some classes that I was struggling in, I joined the Admissions blogger team and started writing high-effort blogs, and I broke up with someone who started talking to another girl five days after the breakup. Moreover, the looming shadow of joblessness began hanging over my head once again.

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that an MIT student in possession of a CS education, must be in want of a technical job. Unfortunately, my freshman summer UROP mentor[18] had ghosted me. I also just found wet lab to be too slow-moving and unpredictable, so I decided to try new projects. The only alternative to wet lab research was obviously computational work, so I attempted to force myself to apply as a software engineer/researcher like everyone else.

None of my applications were successful.

I coped with this by telling myself that Hack was also a resume-line item, and an important one at that; what other opportunity would let you say that you led a 40-person team with a $400k budget while you were still a freshman? But that didn’t erase the awkwardness I’d feel when I wandered through the career fair booths and struggled to name technical classes that I enjoyed, or make me feel proud to hand my sparse resume over to recruiters. I barely understood Python, I didn’t know anything about this AI wave taking the world by storm, and the biopharma companies didn’t take puny little sophomores.

But no matter; I was still a fall semester sophomore. I told myself that I didn’t need to worry about this job stuff right now, and I was just going down a path that wasn’t the conventional path career fair companies wanted. I might not have been the perfect MIT student they wanted, but I’d have time to figure it out… right?

how to say goodbye, part two

After Blueprint, I wrote in an update that I sent to some friends:

blueprint finished 💙 my heart is so, so full. there is a moment where i collapsed onto the chair and looked up at the lights and felt it all come crashing down, but after all of the emotions have left i just feel awash with joy.

when else am i going to call a hackathon so fully mine? so fully ours? the projects were amazing and i feel so impressed and inspired. it all paid off and it was worth it. i think, after all, this event will live in my memory as one of the best things i ever spent six months of my life doing

And with every change of cycle, I said another round of goodbyes. I cried when Maggie and Alison told me that it was time for them to go: I understood that they wanted to spend time on other things, but they had been there from the start, and suddenly I realised that Kimberly[19] and I were the only two from our Hack class[20] still on the team. I felt the same sorrow with Annie,[21] with Claire, with Selena,[22] with everyone else who I’d been through thick and thin with over the past year and a half.

the blueprint 2025 organising team <3

blueprint 2025 heads photo!! i am endlessly grateful to all of my heads for all the sacrifice they did: teresa for battling blender, sophia for all of the finance spreadsheet battles, annie for showing me that being technical is doable as long as you put your mind to it, dom for always being so organised and willing to challenge my decisions, but someone is missing from this...

and sarah was sick because she'd worked so hard at blueprint, but she singlehandedly revamped the sponsorships system and is one of the realest people i know <3 this is some of the heads at ring delivery

With Blueprint wrapped up, I had to think about the big questions left:

How was I going to say goodbye?

how to say goodbye: the beginning of the end

To say goodbye to an institution and help it move on without you, you must set up a legacy. I started looking for a new co-director, and I was left in a conundrum. Somehow, nobody seemed like they really wanted to run for director.

I had conversations with all the eligible fall recruits, and it always felt like there was a missing piece, but I couldn’t quite put a finger on what it was. I started getting really insecure about the way that I had run my Blueprint, because maybe there was an issue with how I had mentored them. I wondered whether the fall kids didn’t want to work with me, whether they thought I complained about the work a little too much, whether they just didn’t believe in the Hack community I’d built. I started spiralling about my leadership abilities and feeling more self-conscious than ever, and I would sit around and complain to my heads and doom about the future of Hack.

As it turned out, my worries were unfounded. When elections came around, two wonderful candidates ran for director. I stressed myself out because I hadn’t seen myself in the fall kids—I hadn’t seen the same desire, the same skillset, the same personality; but you didn’t need to be like me to be a good director. It was too presumptive for me to project my own motivations onto the next generation, and after elections, I was really excited to work with Sanjith for my last HackMIT.

HackMIT 2025: how to get through the last mile

I went into my last HackMIT with a series of expectations based on HackMIT 2024, but I was with a new crowd: a new team, a new set of heads, a new co-director.

Maybe it was because I’d been off Instagram for half a year by then, but I was deeply confused by every online reference that Sanjith pulled out at meetings, while he would roast me for being an unc who sent him facebook reels over Slack. We bantered our way through the onboarding and heads selections, and despite being initially unsettled by his type B approach and brainrot cultural differences, I was soon able to trust and rely on him for when I was spread too thin or when we needed to solve a random issue that popped up. I learned to appreciate his laidback leadership style, which once again reminded me that you didn’t need to be like me to be a good leader. Our committee heads and wider team were also energetic and creative in ways different from HackMIT 2024 that I came to embrace.

sanjith educating the elderly (me) on what is tralalero tralala

srilekha (our wonderful logistics head) and sanjith roasting me for sending them a facebook reel...

after a general team meeting

in one of the marketing meetings designing splash... lauren our wonderful marketing head was very very descriptive

devops and marketing collaborating for website design!

the corporate relations committee deciding sponsorship strategies

We also faced a new set of problems. I was really excited about the energy of our team, and fundraising had gone extremely well due to a combination of the funding landscape and changes in our sponsorship style, so we pushed to scale everything up much more ambitiously. We admitted more people, spent way more money, and set up many more fun perks for the hackers. However, our systems couldn’t adjust to it. We spent days dealing with the fallout from disastrous bugs on our app-reading systems, called up a bunch of last minute merch vendors because of new branding policies, and had to make a last-minute change in judging when our scheduling system broke on the day of HackMIT.

In retrospect, I wish that I’d taken more time to really think about how the systems interacted with each other and designed better contingency plans, but the true lesson here is that organising an event is like playing whack-a-mole: prepare all you want, but new problems will pop up when you least expect it. That’s the fun of it, after all.

Sophomore spring

I loved Hack and its people. Still, after repeating the same playbook for 1.5 years, I started getting tired. I was running the same meetings for the third and even fourth time, saying the same things for the sake of knowledge transfer.

Alright, so for those of you who have done hackathons before, can we popcorn around and talk about what really gives a hackathon their spark? What were the most fun core memories?

No, we can’t try to advertise on this bulletin board, because two years ago we tried this and it
got taken down and we got a talking to…

Let’s talk about how we can improve the sign-in logistical experience! Imagine that you’re a hacker, what would be the easiest sign in workflow…

Now that the novelty of Hack had worn off, I started really feeling the opportunity cost of choosing to spend time on Hack rather than my career. I was committing to research again for the summer, on a more computational bent: I was reasonably excited about what I’d get to learn, but I was also a little disappointed by the fact that none of my internship applications had gone well. Sometimes I felt irritated that I had to work on meeting notes and random logistics while my friends were talking about all of their interviewing and leetcoding and whatever else.

School wasn’t going great either. I got my first B in a class, and then I got another B, and I knew that if I had submitted some more psets on time and studied more, I would have avoided this fate. But there were meetings to attend and tasks to do, and I continued submitting psets in the middle of a meeting and cramming for exams at the very last minute because it was a crunch week for Hack. At this point in college, I’d developed a more calibrated view of what it means to be an MIT student. It’s fine to struggle in your classes, and it’s fine to need a lot of help. But sometimes it felt preventable, and Hack was the reason why I couldn’t do better.

What the older directors had told me about didn’t sink in until now: the last-cycle slog, the accumulation of sacrifices that you make, the moments when you doubt whether this was all worth it. I just had to remind myself: I committed to this not because it was easy, but because I would grow from all the challenges, and I was still learning to prioritise and grow and mature as a leader. We were so close to the finish line, and I was going to see it all through. I represented Hack to so many people—my friends, my team, myself—and Hack was the one thing I really believed in, so if I didn’t organise it the best I could, I wouldn’t be myself anymore.

In the month leading up to HackMIT 2025, most of my frustrations and struggles eventually got resolved. I always found the worst part of planning to be the uncertainty, because it enables the nagging at the back of my mind that I should push harder to find a better option, and overwhelms me with the prospect of an endless option space. But once I make a commitment, I can free myself from my anxieties, and let myself enjoy the ride. I was able to let go of a lot of the leadership baggage and dissatisfaction that I’d collected over my time directing Hack, and it felt like HackMIT 2023 again: the flurry of activity, the excitement that new Hack babies brought, the anticipation of the Event of the Year.

the things you leave behind

Time doesn’t stop for anyone. So, despite all my attempts to savour every moment and hold onto the time I had left as director of Hack, as difficult, fun, painful, fulfilling as it had been, the clock struck midnight and my time came to a close.

the end

A part of me was struck by how different my initial campaign promises were from the hackathons I actually ran. I came into Hack with a lot of drive: I was going to learn all about hackathons, I was going to grow as a leader, and in particular, I was going to lead the club to finish the biggest projects that my predecessors weren’t able to complete.

I wanted to define my time as Hack director through completing two projects: getting overnight venue access for HackMIT again, and seceding from our umbrella organisation to become our own student group. I did everything I could—reaching out to famous alumni and rallying for support, calling emergency meetings and writing up twenty-page pitch documents, burning bridges with leadership—in passionate and sometimes irresponsible ways. At the end of my directorship, neither of the projects came to fruition.

To cope, I had to remind myself that the most important part of the directorship is the hackathon itself, and in that sense, I was happy with what I’d done. I saw first-time teams celebrate their first energy drink (or ten); I saw people tinkering away with hardware they’d never used before because we opened up the makerspaces; I saw bird call classifiers and soil batteries and coordinated cow onesies. I announced that there was a matcha bar and saw the ice rink erupt in joy. I saw old friends and met new faces, and they all hacked and built for the love of the game.

And at the end of my time in Hack, I really did feel like I learned the essence of the hackathon. In my initial post-Hack reflection, I wrote about the part of Hack that I was proudest of:

To be completely honest, by the time the hackathon swung around fully I felt very torn. On the one hand, I was so proud of the work we had done as a team—raising money, coordinating logistics, building platforms, and most visually all the BEAUTIFUL merch and deco that we had done; on the other hand, I felt very disillusioned about the state of the hackathon.

Believe all you want about the idealism of a hackathon—a crazy fun sprint of experimenting and building, hanging out with friends and hacking at a project together, learning to prototype and build—but as an organiser, if you want to understand how people will react to and interact with your hackathon, the clearest way is to distill a hackathon to its functional purpose. Hackathons are often seen by sponsors and hackers as a quirkified career fair. You spend two days to build a demo using [insert LLM coding assistant of choice], and it doesn’t really matter how functional it is, as long as the UI looks good and you can sell the grand potential of the demo. Importantly, this is not a fault of the hackers. If you win the hackathon with that skillset, good for you. We just ran judging in a way that wasn’t aligned to what we value in hackathons.

We tried out a new judging scheme this year, and I’m proud of how it went. The top project was the kind of dream that I think an MIT hackathon deserves: an honest-to-god trashy pitch, but a fully functional product and backend that was hand-written in haskell which rederived gradient descent for non-euclidean distances. Yes, scrappy, nerdy, insane. But that’s the point.

We’re at MIT, after all. I’m at MIT, I ran HackMIT, and I’m so proud of it.

the winners explaining their project

i think this was a visual demo of their gradient descent mechanism

There’s a Chinese saying which has stuck with me: 成长是让人生磨平你的棱角 // growth is accepting that life will smooth out your rough edges. I had plenty of rough edges and ambition when I came into Hack; I wanted to do big projects and revamp everything and work through the last mile because I thought I had the agency and dedication to do so. But life humbles you: I ran into endless obstacles from factors outside of my control, and eventually I had to learn to accept and move on.

With humility comes gratitude, and I have so, so much to be grateful for. For HackMIT 2025, a lot of friends from my prefrosh days came to support—as judges, sponsors, and hackers alike—and they brought flowers, chaos, and memories that imbued so much joy into my final HackMIT. I’ve met countless mentors who have shown me what good leadership looks like, and peers who challenge my decisions and support me when I can’t fix issues myself. I saw our team members grow from fresh-faced Hack babies into the backbones of the team.

With gratitude comes perspective. It was naive for me to promise that I’d deliver what others couldn’t, or act as if I ran MIT’s largest hackathon. It would never be just me who did these things. It was us: it was me and Sanjith, it was the heads, it was each and every single member of the Hack team. It was the predecessors who had set everything up before us. It will be Laura, and all the future co-directors and heads and team members, who will take up the torch. I would not be the one to finish the mission, but I passed my knowledge and ideas onto the next generation, and that will be enough. 前人栽树，后人乘凉 // the predecessor plants the tree, for the successor to take shade beneath.
